stimuli.title: Why batteries get tired
stimuli.text:
**1** Most people have noticed it. A new phone lasts all day on one charge, but two years later it is begging for a charger by lunchtime. The battery has not broken. It has simply aged, and the way we use it decides how fast that happens.

**2** Phones, laptops and electric scooters run on lithium-ion batteries. Inside, tiny charged particles called lithium ions travel from one side of the battery to the other when it charges, and back again when it powers the device. Every trip causes a little wear. Over hundreds of cycles, some of the lithium becomes trapped in a crust that forms on the battery's surfaces, and trapped lithium can no longer carry charge.

**3** Heat speeds this process up. A battery left on the dashboard of a car on a 35-degree day, or charged under a pillow overnight, ages much faster than one kept cool. Charging to 100 per cent and leaving the device plugged in for hours also adds stress, which is why many phones now offer a setting that pauses charging at 80 per cent.

**4** None of this means you should baby your battery. It is designed to be used, and a few hot days will not ruin it. But small habits add up. Keep devices out of direct sun, avoid running the battery completely flat, and unplug when you can. Your battery will still get tired one day; you can simply make that day come later.

stimuli.title: The last ferry
stimuli.text:
Mia heard the horn before she saw the ferry. One long note rolled across the harbour, and her stomach dropped. The last boat to the island left at 6.15, and the clock above the kiosk said 6.13.

She ran. Her school bag thumped against her back, and the bottle of water she had bought for the trip slid out of the side pocket and rolled away under a bench. She let it go.

At the end of the wharf, a deckhand in an orange vest was already lifting the rope from its post. He looked up, saw her coming, and paused with the rope in his hands, the way you might hold a door for someone at the far end of a corridor.

"Big day?" he said as she stumbled aboard.

Mia could only nod. Her chest was burning. She found a seat at the back, beside a man asleep under a newspaper, and watched the city lights shrink behind the boat's white wake. Her mum would be waiting at the island jetty with the car, probably checking her watch.

Later, as the ferry nosed into the jetty, the deckhand passed her seat and dropped something into her lap. It was her water bottle, a little dusty.

"Saw it roll," he said, and was gone before she could thank him.

stimuli.title: Let teenagers sleep
stimuli.text:
**1** Every school morning, thousands of Australian teenagers drag themselves out of bed before their bodies are ready. We tend to blame late nights and screens, and those certainly play a part. But there is a less obvious culprit: biology.

**2** During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts. The hormone that makes us feel sleepy is released later in the evening than it was in childhood, so a typical 15-year-old does not feel tired until around 11 pm. Sleep researchers generally recommend that teenagers get eight to ten hours a night. Do the arithmetic with an alarm set for 6.30 am and the problem is obvious.

**3** Critics argue that a later start would simply push everything back: sport, part-time jobs and family routines would all suffer, and teenagers would stay up later still. These are fair concerns, and any change would need careful planning. Yet schools overseas that have moved their start time by as little as 45 minutes have reported fewer late arrivals and better attendance, and students there say they feel more alert in morning classes.

**4** Nobody is suggesting that a later bell will solve every problem teenagers face. It is, however, one of the few changes that costs almost nothing and works with the body rather than against it. We would never schedule a toddler's nap at midday and then wonder why it went badly. Why do we expect teenagers to learn algebra at a time when their brains are still, in effect, asleep?

stimuli.title: Cooler streets
stimuli.text:
**1** On a summer afternoon, a car park in the middle of a city can be several degrees hotter than a park only a few streets away. This difference is known as the urban heat island effect, and as cities grow and heatwaves become more common, planners are paying it close attention.

**2** The causes are well understood. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly at night, so city temperatures stay high long after sunset. Tall buildings trap warm air and block breezes. Air conditioners, engines and factories add heat of their own. Meanwhile, there are fewer trees and less open soil to cool the air through evaporation.

**3** Some responses are surprisingly simple. Painting roofs in pale colours reflects more sunlight, and trials in several cities have measured lower roof temperatures as a result. Street trees provide shade and release water vapour, and a well-planted street can feel dramatically cooler to someone walking along it. Even replacing a strip of asphalt with grass makes a measurable difference.

**4** The solutions are not without trade-offs, however. Trees need water, which is precious during drought, and their roots can damage pipes and footpaths if the wrong species is chosen. Pale roofs can create glare for neighbours. None of these problems is a reason to do nothing, but they explain why cooling a city is a matter of careful design rather than a single quick fix.

**5** What is clear is that the cost of doing nothing is rising. Heat is a serious health risk, especially for older people and young children, and the hottest suburbs are often those with the least shade. Cooler streets are not a luxury; for many communities they are becoming a necessity.

stimuli.title: Planning a day walk
stimuli.text:
Heading into the bush for a day walk? A little planning keeps a good day from turning into a bad one.

**Before you go**
- Check the weather forecast and any fire danger rating for the area. Do not walk on days of extreme fire danger.
- Choose a track that suits the slowest person in your group.
- Tell someone where you are going and when you expect to be back.

**What to carry**
- At least two litres of water per person, more in hot weather.
- A hat, sunscreen and a warm layer, even in summer.
- A basic first aid kit and a fully charged phone.

**On the track**
Stay on the marked path. Shortcuts damage plants and make it easier to get lost. If you do lose the track, stop, stay calm and stay where you are, because searchers find people faster when they stay put.

stimuli.title: Tryouts
stimuli.text:
Jae had practised his free throws every afternoon for a month. He knew the number by heart: forty-one out of fifty on his best day.

But the gym on tryout day did not feel like his driveway. The lights were too bright, the floor squeaked, and the coach stood at the side with a clipboard, writing without looking up.

His first shot hit the rim and bounced away. So did his second. Jae felt his face go hot. Then he remembered what his older sister had told him: "Breathe out before you shoot. Your arms know what to do."

He breathed out. The ball dropped through the net without touching the rim. He made the next four in a row.

When the list went up on Friday, his name was near the bottom. He read it three times before he believed it.

stimuli.title: When coral turns white
stimuli.text:
**1** From a boat, a healthy coral reef looks like a garden: browns, greens, purples and golds spread across the sea floor. Look closely, though, and the garden is really an animal city. Each coral is a colony of tiny animals called polyps, and most of the colour comes not from the polyps themselves but from microscopic algae living inside their tissue.

**2** The partnership suits both sides. The algae get shelter and the waste products they need, and in return they use sunlight to make food, much of which they pass to the coral. For many reef-building corals, this food supplies most of the energy they need to grow.

**3** The arrangement has one weakness: it works only within a narrow range of temperatures. When the water stays even one or two degrees warmer than usual for several weeks, the algae begin to produce substances that harm the coral, and the coral expels them. Without its algae the coral's white skeleton shows through its clear tissue. This is called bleaching.

**4** A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. If the water cools in time, algae can return and the coral can recover. If the heat lasts too long, the coral dies, and seaweed soon covers the skeleton. Reefs can recover from a single bleaching event over a decade or so, but scientists are concerned that, as ocean temperatures rise, the gaps between events are becoming too short for that recovery to happen.

stimuli.title: Grandad's shed
stimuli.text:
Grandad's shed smelled of sawdust and engine oil, and nobody was allowed in it. That was the rule for as long as I could remember, so when Mum handed me the key the week after the funeral, I held it as if it might bite.

"He'd want someone to sort it," she said. "You were always the one asking what was in there."

The door stuck, then gave with a groan. Inside, everything had a place. Jars of screws were lined up on the shelves, sorted by size. Chisels hung on nails, their outlines traced in black marker on the wall behind them, so you could see at a glance which one was missing. None were.

On the bench, under a dust sheet, I found a wooden box with my name burned into the lid. It was nearly finished. The hinges were fitted, the corners joined so neatly that I could not feel the seams. Only the clasp was missing, and beside the box, in Grandad's square handwriting, was a note: *Brass clasp, second drawer. Show her how.*

I opened the second drawer. The clasp was there, wrapped in a rag, with four tiny screws. I sat down on his stool and, for the first time, understood that the rule had never been about keeping me out. He had just been waiting until it was ready.

stimuli.title: Fix it, don't bin it
stimuli.text:
**1** Last month my toaster stopped working. A neighbour who repairs appliances as a hobby took it apart on her kitchen table, found a loose wire, and had it working again in ten minutes. The shop where I bought it had told me it was not worth repairing and offered me a discount on a new one.

**2** That gap, between what can be fixed and what we are told is worth fixing, is the heart of the right-to-repair debate. Manufacturers increasingly glue parts together, use unusual screws, or refuse to sell spare parts and repair manuals to anyone but their own technicians. The result is that a small fault often means a whole product goes to landfill.

**3** Manufacturers argue that some restrictions protect customers. A badly repaired heater or phone battery can be dangerous, and companies do not want to be blamed for an amateur's mistake. That argument deserves respect, but it does not explain why a simple toaster needs special tools to open, or why a spare part costs more than half the price of a new machine.

**4** Repair is not just about saving money. Every product that is fixed instead of replaced means fewer raw materials dug up, less energy used in factories and less waste. Community repair cafes, where volunteers teach people to mend their own things, are popping up in town halls and libraries around the country, and they are rarely short of customers.

**5** We do not need to become experts. We just need products designed so that experts, and curious neighbours, can get inside them.

stimuli.title: Low tide
stimuli.text:
The sea has gone out for the afternoon,
like a guest who leaves the table mid-sentence,
and the rocks it left behind lie bare and shining,
a city with its roof lifted off.

In every pool a small world carries on:
a crab rehearses its sideways argument,
anemones close their fists on nothing,
a periwinkle writes its slow line in the sand.

I crouch and do not touch.
The light moves, the water shivers,
and far off, quietly, the sea
is already deciding to come back.

stimuli.title: Town library notice
stimuli.text: From 1 July, the town library will open on Sundays from 10 am to 3 pm. The change follows a survey in which more than half of the people who answered said that weekday opening hours did not suit them. To keep costs the same, the library will close at 5 pm on Mondays instead of 8 pm. Late returns can still be left in the drop box at the front door at any time.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of this text?
options: Batteries wear out with use, and some habits slow that wear down.
Phone makers design batteries to stop working after two years.
Lithium-ion batteries are dangerous when they get too hot.
Charging a phone overnight will break its battery.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the battery 'has simply aged' and that 'the way we use it decides how fast that happens'; the rest explains the wear and the habits that slow it. Nothing says batteries are designed to fail, and paragraph 4 says a few hot days 'will not ruin it'.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why does a battery hold less charge over time?
options: The lithium ions stop moving once the battery is full.
Some lithium gets trapped and can no longer carry charge.
The battery leaks lithium each time it is charged.
The crust on the surfaces makes the battery heavier.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says lithium 'becomes trapped in a crust' and 'trapped lithium can no longer carry charge'. The crust traps lithium; the text says nothing about weight or leaking.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention a phone 'charged under a pillow overnight'?
options: To warn that phones can start fires in bedrooms
To show that most people charge their phones at night
As an example of a habit that exposes a battery to heat
As an example of the 80 per cent charging setting
questions.explanation: The sentence before it says 'Heat speeds this process up', and the pillow, like the hot dashboard, traps heat. The text does not discuss fires.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the writer says 'None of this means you should baby your battery.' What does 'baby' mean here?
questions.explanation: To baby something is to protect it more than it needs. The next sentence, 'It is designed to be used', confirms that the writer means people should not be overly careful.

questions.stem: Which two pieces of advice does the writer give? Choose two.
options: Always charge the battery to 100 per cent.
Keep devices out of direct sun.
Let the battery run completely flat once a month.
Store the phone in a car in summer.
Unplug the device when you can.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 advises keeping devices out of direct sun and unplugging when you can. It says to avoid running the battery flat, and paragraph 3 warns that charging to 100 per cent adds stress.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happen in the story.
options: Mia's water bottle rolls under a bench.
The deckhand pauses with the rope in his hands.
The deckhand asks Mia if it is a big day.
The deckhand drops the bottle in Mia's lap.
questions.explanation: The story runs in time order: the horn, the run (when the bottle falls), the deckhand waiting with the rope, his question as she boards, and the bottle returned at the island jetty.

questions.stem: Why does Mia's 'stomach drop' when she hears the horn?
options: She is afraid of travelling on boats.
She fears she will miss the last ferry.
She has lost her school bag.
She knows her mum is angry with her.
questions.explanation: The next sentences explain it: the last boat leaves at 6.15 and the clock says 6.13. Her fear is about the time, not the boat.

questions.stem: The deckhand pauses 'the way you might hold a door for someone at the far end of a corridor'. What does this comparison suggest about him?
options: He is annoyed that she is running late.
He does not notice her coming.
He is being kind by waiting for her.
He is about to close the gate on her.
questions.explanation: Holding a door for someone is a small courtesy. The comparison shows he chooses to wait, which fits his later kindness with the bottle.

questions.stem: What does the ending suggest about the deckhand?
options: He wanted Mia to thank him in front of others.
He took the bottle by mistake.
He is a friend of Mia's mother.
He notices small things and helps without fuss.
questions.explanation: He saw the bottle roll, picked it up and returned it, then 'was gone before she could thank him'. He did not wait for thanks.

questions.stem: Which word best describes Mia when she boards the ferry?
questions.explanation: 'Mia could only nod. Her chest was burning.' She has run the length of the wharf and cannot speak.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of this text?
options: To describe the writer's favourite walk
To help people plan a safe day walk
To warn people never to walk alone
questions.explanation: The headings 'Before you go', 'What to carry' and 'On the track' are all practical advice for a day walk.

questions.stem: How much water should each person carry, at the least?
questions.explanation: Under 'What to carry': 'At least two litres of water per person, more in hot weather.'

questions.stem: Why does the text say to choose a track that suits 'the slowest person in your group'?
options: So that everyone can finish safely
So that the walk takes as long as possible
So that fast walkers can go ahead alone
So that the group always walks on flat ground
questions.explanation: If the track suits the slowest walker, nobody is left behind or pushed beyond what they can do. Nothing in the text suggests splitting up.

questions.stem: What should you do if you lose the track?
options: Walk downhill until you find water.
Stop and stay where you are.
Take a shortcut back to the car park.
Keep walking until your phone has signal.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph: 'stop, stay calm and stay where you are, because searchers find people faster when they stay put'.

questions.stem: Why is the information organised under headings with dot points?
options: So the text sounds like a story
So the writer can give an opinion
So readers can find advice quickly
So the most important rule comes last
questions.explanation: Headings and dot points break advice into stages (before, carry, on the track) so a reader can scan for what they need.

questions.stem: Why does Jae know the number 'forty-one out of fifty' by heart?
options: It was the number of players at the tryout.
It was the score the coach wrote down.
It was the number on his team shirt.
It was his best free-throw score.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says he practised every afternoon and 'forty-one out of fifty' was 'on his best day'.

questions.stem: Why did the gym 'not feel like his driveway'?
options: It felt strange, and he was watched.
It was smaller than his driveway.
His sister was not allowed inside.
questions.explanation: The bright lights, squeaking floor and the coach with a clipboard make the gym strange and stressful compared with practising at home.

questions.stem: 'Jae felt his face go hot.' What does this tell you about how he felt?
questions.explanation: His face goes hot straight after two missed shots in front of the coach. A hot face is a common sign of embarrassment.

questions.stem: What helped Jae make his shots after the first two misses?
options: The coach telling him to slow down
His sister's advice to breathe out
questions.explanation: He 'remembered what his older sister had told him', breathed out, and then made five shots in a row.

questions.stem: Why did Jae read the list 'three times before he believed it'?
options: He could not find his name at first.
He was checking which friends had made it.
He was surprised that he had made the team.
questions.explanation: His name is on the list, near the bottom. Reading it again and again shows he could hardly believe he had been picked after a nervous start.

questions.stem: What is the writer's main purpose in this text?
options: To explain how the body's internal clock works
To persuade readers that schools should start later
To describe a school that changed its start time
To argue that teenagers should use screens less
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 makes the case directly ('one of the few changes that costs almost nothing'), and the closing question challenges readers. The biology in paragraph 2 is evidence for that argument, not the purpose itself.

questions.stem: How is paragraph 3 different from the other paragraphs?
options: It gives the scientific cause of the problem.
It tells a personal story about the writer.
It presents an opposing view before answering it.
It summarises the argument of the whole text.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 opens with 'Critics argue', concedes 'These are fair concerns', then answers with 'Yet' and the evidence from schools overseas. That is a counter-argument and rebuttal.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the writer says 'Do the arithmetic with an alarm set for 6.30 am'. What point is the writer making?
options: Teenagers need to be better at maths before school starts.
Most teenagers set their alarms too late.
An alarm at 6.30 am gives exactly the recommended amount of sleep.
Sleeping from 11 pm to 6.30 am is not enough sleep.
questions.explanation: From 11 pm to 6.30 am is seven and a half hours, less than the eight to ten hours recommended. The writer leaves readers to work this out.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention a toddler's nap in paragraph 4?
options: To make the school timetable seem as unwise as a badly timed nap
To show that young children also need more sleep than adults
To suggest that schools should offer students an afternoon rest
To prove that the body clock changes during adolescence
questions.explanation: The writer uses the absurd image of a badly timed nap to make the current school timetable seem equally unreasonable. It is an analogy, not evidence about toddlers' sleep.

questions.stem:
Which sentence from the text gives evidence from real schools? Select it.

{{We tend to blame late nights and screens, and those certainly play a part.}} {{Sleep researchers generally recommend that teenagers get eight to ten hours a night.}} {{Yet schools overseas that have moved their start time by as little as 45 minutes have reported fewer late arrivals and better attendance.}} {{Nobody is suggesting that a later bell will solve every problem teenagers face.}}
questions.explanation: Only the third sentence reports results from schools that actually changed their start time. The second is a recommendation from researchers, not evidence from schools.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why do cities stay hot after sunset?
options: Air conditioners are switched off at night.
Roads and roofs release stored heat.
Tall buildings block the cool evening sun.
Trees release warm water vapour at night.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: dark roads and roofs 'release the stored heat slowly at night, so city temperatures stay high long after sunset'.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of paragraph 4?
options: To argue that cities should not plant more trees
To list the causes of the urban heat island effect
To show that the cooling methods have drawbacks to manage
To explain why pale roofs do not work
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 opens 'The solutions are not without trade-offs' and ends that the problems are not 'a reason to do nothing'. It qualifies the solutions rather than rejecting them.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does 'trade-offs' mean?
options: drawbacks that come with a benefit
questions.explanation: A trade-off is something you give up to gain something else. The paragraph lists drawbacks (water use, root damage, glare) that come with each cooling method.

questions.stem: Which two statements would the writer most likely agree with? Choose two.
options: Painting roofs white is the only change cities need.
Choosing the right tree species matters.
Heat islands affect only people who live in the city centre.
Shade is unevenly shared between suburbs.
Cities should wait until droughts end before planting trees.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 warns about 'the wrong species', and paragraph 5 says 'the hottest suburbs are often those with the least shade'. The writer rejects 'a single quick fix' and says problems are not 'a reason to do nothing'.

questions.stem: What is the tone of the final paragraph?
questions.explanation: Phrases such as 'the cost of doing nothing is rising', 'a serious health risk' and 'becoming a necessity' press the reader to act. The earlier paragraphs are more neutral and explanatory.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Necessary has one c and a double s: ne-c-e-ss-ary. A memory trick: one collar, two sleeves.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The students were asked to [[1]] their recycling into three bins.
questions.explanation: Separate has 'par' in the middle: se-par-ate. 'Seperate' is one of the most common misspellings in English.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

The {{coach}} said our {{team}} would {{definately}} {{play}} in the {{final}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'definitely': it is built on 'finite', so it has i, i and an e at the end.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: After c, the e comes before the i: receive, ceiling, deceive.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The new library will be open from the [[1]] of March.
questions.explanation: Begin ends in a stressed short vowel and one consonant, so the n doubles before -ing: beginning.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

It was {{embarassing}} when my {{phone}} rang {{during}} the {{quiet}} {{assembly}}.
questions.explanation: Embarrassing has a double r and a double s. Think 'really red, so shy'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The box of old photos [[1]] in the hallway cupboard.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'box', which is singular; 'of old photos' only describes it. A singular subject takes 'is'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The bus was late so, we missed the start of the film.
The bus was late, so we missed the start of the film.
The bus was late, so, we missed the start of the film.
The bus was late so we missed, the start of the film.
questions.explanation: When 'so' joins two complete clauses, the comma goes before it. No comma follows 'so'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

All of the [[1]] lockers were painted over the holidays.
questions.explanation: The lockers belong to many students. For a plural ending in s, the apostrophe goes after the s: students'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

By the time the firefighters arrived, the fire [[1]] already spread to the shed.
questions.explanation: The spreading happened before the firefighters arrived, which is already in the past. An earlier past action takes the past perfect: had spread.

questions.stem:
Which word in this sentence is a conjunction?

Although it was raining, the match went ahead.
questions.explanation: 'Although' joins the subordinate clause 'it was raining' to the main clause. A conjunction links clauses.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The coach gave the trophy to Priya and [[1]].
questions.explanation: After 'to', use the object pronoun 'me'. Test it by removing Priya: 'gave the trophy to me', not 'to I'.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: I before e except after c: believe. 'Never believe a lie' helps, since 'lie' sits inside believe.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

We will finish the project [[1]].
questions.explanation: Tomorrow has one m and a double r.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

My {{freind}} {{brought}} her {{dog}} to the {{beach}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'friend'. A trick: you will be friends to the end, so the word ends in -end.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Library has two rs: li-brar-y. Say it slowly to hear both.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

Mum asked me to put the plates in the [[1]].
questions.explanation: Cupboard is a compound word: cup + board, even though the p is silent when we say it.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

We {{waited}} {{untill}} the {{rain}} {{stopped}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'until', with one l. 'Till' has two, but 'until' does not.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

My brother and I [[1]] going to the show on Saturday.
questions.explanation: 'My brother and I' is two people, a plural subject, so the verb is 'are'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: We bought bread milk, eggs and apples.
We bought bread, milk, eggs and apples.
We bought, bread, milk, eggs and apples.
We bought bread, milk eggs, and apples.
questions.explanation: Commas separate the items in a list. No comma goes between the verb 'bought' and the list.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

Last week the class [[1]] a new captain.
questions.explanation: 'Last week' puts the action in the past. 'Choose' is irregular: its simple past is 'chose'. 'Chosen' needs a helper verb (has chosen), and 'choosed' is not a word.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The [[1]] books are on the bottom shelf.
questions.explanation: 'Children' is already plural without an s, so add apostrophe s to show the books belong to them: children's. 'Childrens' is not a word.

questions.stem:
Which word in this sentence should start with a capital letter?

At the festival we tried some japanese food.
questions.explanation: 'Japanese' comes from the name of a country, Japan, so it is a proper adjective and takes a capital letter. 'Festival' and 'food' are common nouns.

questions.stem:
Which word is an adjective in this sentence?

The tired runners crossed the line.
questions.explanation: An adjective describes a noun. 'Tired' describes the runners.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Accommodation has a double c and a double m: it accommodates both.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

The {{committee}} gave {{priority}} to {{maintainance}} of the {{existing}} {{buildings}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'maintenance'. The verb is 'maintain', but the noun drops the i: main-ten-ance.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The flooding was an unusual [[1]] for a town so far from the coast.
questions.explanation: Occur ends in a stressed vowel and one r, so the r doubles: occurrence. The ending is -ence, as in 'difference'.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Conscientious keeps 'science' in the middle: con-science-tious, with -tious at the end.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

The {{speech}} was {{persuasive}}, but some {{statements}} were {{irrelevent}} to the {{topic}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'irrelevant': ir + relevant, and relevant ends in -ant.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The band kept a steady [[1]] all through the song.
questions.explanation: Rhythm has no vowel except the y: r-h-y-t-h-m. 'Rhythm helps your two hips move' gives the letters.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The results were clear, the new design used less energy.
The results were clear; and the new design used less energy.
The results were clear; the new design used less energy.
The results were; clear the new design used less energy.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences without a conjunction. A comma alone between them is a comma splice.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

Neither the captain nor the players [[1]] happy with the umpire's decision.
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Players' is plural, so the verb is 'were'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The kit had three parts: a tent, a stove and a water filter.
The kit had: three parts, a tent, a stove and a water filter.
The kit had three parts; a tent, a stove and a water filter.
The kit had three parts, a tent: a stove and a water filter.
questions.explanation: A colon introduces a list after a complete clause ('The kit had three parts'). A colon should not split a verb from its object.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The scientist [[1]] research changed the treatment of burns was invited to speak.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows that the research belongs to the scientist. 'Who's' means 'who is'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: "We leave at dawn" said the guide, "so pack tonight."
"We leave at dawn," said the guide, "So pack tonight."
"We leave at dawn," said the guide, "so pack tonight."
"We leave at dawn," said the guide. "so pack tonight."
questions.explanation: The comma after 'dawn' goes inside the speech marks. The sentence continues after 'said the guide', so a comma follows and 'so' stays lower case.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the passive voice?
options: The mayor will open the bridge.
The mayor was opening the bridge.
The bridge was opened by the mayor.
questions.explanation: In the passive voice the thing acted on (the bridge) is the subject, and the doer comes after 'by'. 'Was opening' is active: the mayor is still doing it.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{6}$? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explanation: Use the common denominator 12: $\frac{9}{12} + \frac{2}{12} = \frac{11}{12}$. Adding tops and bottoms ($\frac{4}{10}$) is the usual slip.

questions.stem: What is $0.6 \times 0.4$?
questions.explanation: $6 \times 4 = 24$, and there are two decimal places in the question, so the answer is 0.24.

questions.stem: What is $-7 + 3 \times (-2)$?
questions.explanation: Multiply first: $3 \times (-2) = -6$. Then $-7 + (-6) = -13$. Working left to right gives $(-4) \times (-2) = 8$, which ignores the order of operations.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 240?
Which is closest to $49.8 \times 20.3$?
questions.explanation: Round to $50 \times 20 = 1000$.

questions.stem: What is $2^3 \times 3^2$?
A phone plan costs \$35 a month. How much does it cost for a year, in dollars?
questions.explanation: $35 \times 12 = 420$ dollars.

questions.stem: A rectangular garden bed is 3.5 m long and 1.2 m wide. What is its area, in square metres?
questions.explanation: Area $= 3.5 \times 1.2 = 4.2$ m². Adding the two sides gives 4.7, which is half the perimeter, not the area.

questions.stem: The ages of six players in a team are 14, 15, 15, 16, 17 and 19. What is their mean age?
Solve $3x - 7 = 20$.
questions.explanation: Add 7 to both sides: $3x = 27$. Divide by 3: $x = 9$. Stopping at $3x = 27$ gives the distractor 27.

questions.stem: Two angles of a triangle are $48^\circ$ and $67^\circ$. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$: $180 - 48 - 67 = 65$. $115^\circ$ is the sum of the two given angles.

questions.stem: A school has 480 students. The ratio of students who walk to those who do not is 3 : 5. How many students walk?
questions.explanation: There are $3 + 5 = 8$ parts, so one part is $480 \div 8 = 60$ students. Walkers are $3 \times 60 = 180$.

questions.stem: A bag holds 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green counters. One counter is taken at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are $3 + 5 + 2 = 10$ counters and 5 are blue, so $P = \frac{5}{10} = \frac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 9 cm and 12 cm. How long is the hypotenuse, in centimetres?
Which expression is equal to $a^5 \times a^3$?
questions.explanation: When multiplying powers of the same base, add the indices: $5 + 3 = 8$. Multiplying the indices gives $a^{15}$, a common error.

questions.stem:
A class surveyed how students get to school.

| | Walk | Bus | Car |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year 9A | 8 | 12 | 6 |
| Year 9B | 11 | 7 | 9 |

Is each statement true or false?
rows: Bus is the most common way for 9A.
The two classes have the same number of students.
questions.explanation: 9B has 11 walkers and 9A has 8, so the first is true. Bus (12) is 9A's largest number, so the second is true. 9A has $8 + 12 + 6 = 26$ students and 9B has $11 + 7 + 9 = 27$, so the third is false.

questions.stem: A map has a scale of 1 : 50 000. Two towns are 6 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
questions.explanation: $6 \times 50\,000 = 300\,000$ cm. There are 100 000 cm in a kilometre, so the distance is 3 km.

questions.stem: A jacket was \$120. In a sale its price fell to \$90. What was the percentage decrease?
questions.explanation: The decrease is \$30, and $\frac{30}{120} = 0.25 = 25\%$. Dividing by the new price, $\frac{30}{90}$, gives about 33%.

questions.stem: Bananas cost \$3.80 per kilogram. How much do 2.5 kg cost, in dollars?
questions.explanation: $3.80 \times 2.5 = 9.50$ dollars.

questions.stem: How many millilitres are in 2.4 litres?
questions.explanation: There are 1000 mL in a litre, so $2.4 \times 1000 = 2400$ mL.

questions.stem: What is the median of 4, 9, 2, 7 and 5?
questions.explanation: In order: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. The middle value is 5.

questions.stem: Solve $x + 14 = 32$.
questions.explanation: Subtract 14 from both sides: $x = 32 - 14 = 18$.

questions.stem: A square has a perimeter of 36 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres?
questions.explanation: Each side is $36 \div 4 = 9$ cm, and the area is $9 \times 9 = 81$ cm².

questions.stem: What is 35% of \$80, in dollars?
questions.explanation: $0.35 \times 80 = 28$ dollars.

questions.stem: A spinner has 4 equal sections numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4. What is the chance of spinning an even number?
questions.explanation: 2 and 4 are even: 2 sections out of 4, which is $\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: Two angles make a straight line. One is $125^\circ$. What is the other?
questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add to $180^\circ$: $180 - 125 = 55$.

questions.stem: The temperature at 6 am was $-4^\circ$C. By noon it had risen $11^\circ$C. What was the temperature at noon?
questions.explanation: $-4 + 11 = 7$, so it was $7^\circ$C.

questions.stem:
Daily top temperatures for a week, in degrees Celsius:

| Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat | Sun |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24 | 27 | 31 | 22 | 25 | 29 | 26 |

What is the range of these temperatures?
questions.explanation: Range $= \text{highest} - \text{lowest} = 31 - 22 = 9$.

questions.stem: A train leaves at 10.45 am and arrives at 1.20 pm. How long is the trip?
questions.explanation: 10.45 am to 12.45 pm is 2 hours, and 12.45 pm to 1.20 pm is 35 minutes.

questions.stem: If $n = 6$, what is the value of $4n - 5$?
questions.explanation: Substitute: $4 \times 6 - 5 = 24 - 5 = 19$. Reading $4n$ as 46 gives 41.

questions.stem: \$2500 is invested at 4% per year simple interest. How much interest is earned in 3 years, in dollars?
questions.explanation: Simple interest $= P \times r \times t = 2500 \times 0.04 \times 3 = 300$ dollars.

questions.stem: A cylindrical water tank has a radius of 1.5 m and a height of 2 m. What is its volume, in cubic metres, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: $V = \pi r^2 h = \pi \times 1.5^2 \times 2 = 4.5\pi \approx 14.1$ m³.

questions.stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the total is 9?
questions.explanation: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. A total of 9 comes from (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4) and (6, 3): 4 outcomes, and $\frac{4}{36} = \frac{1}{9}$.

questions.stem: Which is $0.000\,47$ written in scientific notation?
questions.explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places right to get 4.7, so the power is $10^{-4}$. $47 \times 10^{-5}$ has the right value but is not in scientific notation, since 47 is not between 1 and 10.

questions.stem: A ladder 5 m long leans against a wall. Its foot is 1.4 m from the wall on flat ground. How high up the wall does it reach, in metres?
questions.explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse: $h^2 = 5^2 - 1.4^2 = 25 - 1.96 = 23.04$, so $h = 4.8$ m.

questions.stem: Expand and simplify $3(2x - 5) - 2(x - 4)$.
The mean of five test scores is 72. Four of the scores are 65, 70, 78 and 80. What is the fifth score?
questions.explanation: The five scores total $5 \times 72 = 360$. The four known scores total 293, so the fifth is $360 - 293 = 67$.

questions.stem: A closed box (rectangular prism) is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. What is its total surface area?
questions.explanation: The faces come in pairs: $2(4 \times 3) + 2(4 \times 2) + 2(3 \times 2) = 24 + 16 + 12 = 52$ cm². 24 is the volume in cm³, and 26 counts each pair once.

questions.stem: A line passes through the points $(1, 4)$ and $(5, 12)$. What is its gradient?
questions.explanation: Gradient $= \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{12 - 4}{5 - 1} = \frac{8}{4} = 2$.

questions.stem: In a group of 30 students, 18 play sport, 12 play music and 5 do both. How many students do neither?
questions.explanation: Students who do at least one: $18 + 12 - 5 = 25$ (the 5 who do both were counted twice). Neither: $30 - 25 = 5$.

questions.stem: Two triangles are similar. A side of 6 cm in the small triangle matches a side of 15 cm in the large one. The small triangle has another side of 4 cm. How long is the matching side in the large triangle?
questions.explanation: The scale factor is $15 \div 6 = 2.5$, so the side is $4 \times 2.5 = 10$ cm. Adding the difference, $4 + 9$, gives 13 cm, which is not how similar shapes scale.

questions.stem: Solve $\frac{2x + 3}{5} = 7$.
questions.explanation: Multiply both sides by 5: $2x + 3 = 35$. Subtract 3: $2x = 32$. Divide by 2: $x = 16$.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, why does the writer say the reef is 'really an animal city'?
options: Each coral is a colony of animals.
Many fish and crabs live on the reef.
Reefs are found close to large cities.
The reef is shaped like a city skyline.
questions.explanation: The next sentence explains it: 'Each coral is a colony of tiny animals called polyps.' The garden comparison describes how it looks; the city comparison describes what it is.

questions.stem: What does the coral give the algae?
options: shelter and waste products they need
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'The algae get shelter and the waste products they need.' Food made from sunlight is what the algae give the coral.

questions.stem: Why does a bleached coral look white?
options: The heat burns the colour out of its tissue.
Seaweed covers it with a white coating.
Without the algae, its white skeleton shows through.
The polyps produce a white substance to cool down.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'Without its algae the coral's white skeleton shows through its clear tissue.' Most of its colour came from the algae.

questions.stem: Put the stages of a bleaching event in order.
options: The water stays warmer than usual for weeks.
The algae start producing harmful substances.
The coral starves and turns white.
If the heat lasts, seaweed covers the dead coral.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 3 and 4 give the chain: warm water, harmful substances, the algae expelled, a white starving coral, then death and seaweed if the heat lasts.

questions.stem: What is the main concern the writer raises in paragraph 4?
options: Seaweed is spreading faster than coral grows.
Scientists cannot tell bleached coral from dead coral.
Reefs may not have time to recover between bleaching events.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says reefs can recover 'over a decade or so', but 'the gaps between events are becoming too short for that recovery to happen'. It says bleached coral can recover if the water cools.

questions.stem: Why does the narrator hold the key 'as if it might bite'?
options: The shed was always off limits.
The key is old and sharp.
She is afraid of what her mum will say.
She thinks the shed is dangerous.
questions.explanation: The shed was off limits 'for as long as I could remember', so being handed the key feels strange and almost forbidden.

questions.stem: What do the traced outlines of the chisels suggest about Grandad?
options: He wanted to sell his tools.
He did not trust other people.
questions.explanation: Everything 'had a place', the screws were sorted by size, and the outlines showed at a glance if a chisel was missing. 'None were.' This all shows a careful, orderly man.

questions.stem: What does the note on the bench tell the reader?
options: Grandad wanted the box to be sold.
Grandad had forgotten where the clasp was.
Grandad meant to finish it with her.
Grandad wanted Mum to finish the box.
questions.explanation: 'Show her how' tells someone to teach 'her' to fit the clasp. The box has the narrator's name on it, so the plan was to finish it together.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the narrator's realisation at the end?
options: Grandad had never liked visitors in his shed.
The box would never be finished.
Mum had known about the box all along.
The rule was about waiting, not keeping her out.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the rule 'had never been about keeping me out. He had just been waiting until it was ready.'

questions.stem: The door 'stuck, then gave with a groan'. Why does the writer include this detail?
options: To show the shed has not been used lately
To show that the narrator is weak
To suggest that someone is inside
To show that Grandad built the door badly
questions.explanation: A stuck, groaning door suggests disuse, fitting the week since the funeral. The rest of the shed shows Grandad built things carefully, so poor workmanship does not fit.

questions.stem: Why does the writer begin with the story of the toaster?
options: To complain about a neighbour's hobby
To give a real example of the problem
To show that toasters are badly made
questions.explanation: The anecdote sets up paragraph 2's 'gap, between what can be fixed and what we are told is worth fixing'.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, which two things do some manufacturers do that make repair harder? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists gluing parts, unusual screws, and refusing to sell spare parts and manuals. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.stem: How does the writer respond to the manufacturers' safety argument in paragraph 3?
options: Agrees with it and changes position
Ignores it and changes the subject
Accepts part of it, then shows its limits
questions.explanation: 'That argument deserves respect, but it does not explain' the toaster or the price of parts. This is a concession followed by a rebuttal.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what is the purpose of mentioning repair cafes?
options: To show there is demand for repair
To show that repair is only for experts
To explain how to start a repair cafe
To argue that libraries should close
questions.explanation: Cafes are 'popping up' around the country and 'rarely short of customers', which is evidence of demand for repair.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up the writer's position?
options: Everyone should learn to repair their own appliances.
Products should be designed to be repaired.
Manufacturers should stop selling new products.
Repairs should be done only by company technicians.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph: 'We do not need to become experts. We just need products designed so that experts, and curious neighbours, can get inside them.'

questions.stem: In the first stanza, the sea is compared to 'a guest who leaves the table mid-sentence'. What does this suggest?
options: The sea is rude and unwelcome.
The sea is talking to the rocks.
The sea left suddenly and will return.
The sea leaves because it is bored.
questions.explanation: A guest who leaves mid-sentence has not finished and is expected back, which matches the last line, 'already deciding to come back'.

questions.stem: What is the 'city with its roof lifted off'?
options: a town built beside the beach
questions.explanation: The line describes 'the rocks it left behind', now bare. With the water gone you can see into the pools, like looking into a city from above.

questions.stem: 'a crab rehearses its sideways argument' is an example of
questions.explanation: Rehearsing an argument is a human action given to a crab. The phrase does not rhyme, and the words do not share opening sounds.

questions.stem: What does the line 'I crouch and do not touch' show about the speaker?
questions.explanation: The speaker watches closely but chooses not to disturb the 'small world'. Nothing suggests fear or collecting.

questions.stem: How does the final stanza change the mood of the poem?
options: It turns the poem into a joke.
It hints that the moment will not last.
It shows the speaker is lost.
questions.explanation: The light moves, the water shivers and the sea 'is already deciding to come back', reminding the reader that the low tide is brief. The tone stays calm, not frightening.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Government is built from 'govern' + '-ment', so the n stays: govern-ment.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

The {{weather}} {{forecast}} said the {{temprature}} would {{reach}} {{thirty}} degrees.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'temperature': tem-per-a-ture. The 'per' is often swallowed when people say it.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

She was [[1]] by how quickly the tickets sold out.
questions.explanation: Surprise has two rs: sur-prise. The 'sur' is the same as in 'surface'.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Environment keeps the n from 'environ': environ + ment.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The crowd was [[1]] when the concert was cancelled.
questions.explanation: Disappointed is dis + appointed: one s from 'dis', then the double p of 'appoint'.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

The {{athletes}} showed {{great}} {{disipline}} in {{training}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'discipline': d-i-s-c-i-p-l-i-n-e. The sc is like the sc in 'science'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

Each of the paintings [[1]] a small label underneath it.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'each', which is singular, so the verb is 'has'. 'Of the paintings' does not change the subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Our neighbour who grows tomatoes, gave us a box of them.
Our neighbour, who grows tomatoes gave us a box of them.
Our neighbour who, grows tomatoes, gave us a box of them.
Our neighbour, who grows tomatoes, gave us a box of them.
questions.explanation: 'Who grows tomatoes' is extra information, so it is set off by a pair of commas, one on each side.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

If I [[1]] more time, I would finish the model tonight.
questions.explanation: This is an imagined situation ('I would finish'), so the if-clause takes the past tense: if I had.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

[[1]] going to be a long drive, so bring a book.
questions.explanation: 'It's' is short for 'it is': it is going to be a long drive. 'Its' shows belonging, like 'his' or 'her'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: The bell rang and everyone left.
When the bell rang, everyone left.
questions.explanation: A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause. 'When the bell rang' cannot stand alone and depends on 'everyone left'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The teacher spoke [[1]] so that the baby next door would not wake.
questions.explanation: An adverb is needed to describe how the teacher spoke: quietly. 'Quiet' is an adjective.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Parliament has an i before the a: par-lia-ment.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The road works were only [[1]], so the old surface was back within a year.
questions.explanation: Temporary is tem-por-ar-y, related to 'temporal'. The middle 'or' is often dropped in speech.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

The {{company}} offered a {{guarentee}} that {{every}} {{repair}} would {{last}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'guarantee': g-u-a-r-a-n-t-e-e. The u is silent, as in 'guard'.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Mischievous has three syllables: mis-chie-vous. There is no i before the -ous.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The artist was [[1]] for her use of colour.
questions.explanation: Acknowledged is ac + knowledge + d. It keeps the c before the k and the d before the ge of knowledge.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

It is {{noticable}} that {{fewer}} {{people}} {{visit}} in {{winter}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'noticeable'. The e of 'notice' stays before -able to keep the c soft.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The forecast was poor; however, the race went ahead.
The forecast was poor, however the race went ahead.
The forecast was poor however, the race went ahead.
The forecast was poor; however the race, went ahead.
questions.explanation: 'However' is not a conjunction, so it cannot join two sentences with a comma. Use a semicolon before it and a comma after.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The number of students who walk to school [[1]] risen this year.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the number', which is singular, so the verb is 'has'. 'A number of students have' would be plural, but 'the number' is not.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The prize will go to [[1]] finishes the puzzle first.
questions.explanation: 'Whoever' is the subject of 'finishes'. The whole clause is the object of 'to', but inside it 'whoever' does the finishing.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: My aunt lives in: three places, Darwin in winter, Hobart in summer and Adelaide in between.
My aunt lives in three places; Darwin in winter, Hobart in summer and Adelaide in between.
My aunt lives, in three places: Darwin in winter, Hobart in summer and Adelaide in between.
My aunt lives in three places: Darwin in winter, Hobart in summer and Adelaide in between.
questions.explanation: A colon after the complete clause 'My aunt lives in three places' introduces the list. A semicolon cannot introduce a list.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a modal verb to show the strongest obligation?
options: Visitors must sign in at the office.
Visitors might sign in at the office.
Visitors could sign in at the office.
Visitors may sign in at the office.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses a requirement. 'Might', 'could' and 'may' express possibility or permission.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

Having finished the test early, [[1]].
blanks: every answer was checked by Sam
questions.explanation: The opening phrase describes who finished early, so that person must come straight after the comma. Otherwise the phrase dangles: the answers did not finish the test.

questions.stem: What is $2\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{5}$?
What is $3.2 \div 0.04$?
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by 100: $320 \div 4 = 80$.

questions.stem: A shirt costs \$40. It is reduced by 25%. What is the new price, in dollars?
questions.explanation: 25% of \$40 is \$10, so the new price is \$30.

questions.stem: Which fraction is the largest?
What is $\sqrt{144} + \sqrt{25}$?
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{144} = 12$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$, so the sum is 17.
Subtract $2x$ from both sides: $3x + 4 = 19$. Subtract 4: $3x = 15$. Divide by 3: $x = 5$.

questions.stem: A triangle has a base of 14 cm and a perpendicular height of 9 cm. What is its area, in square centimetres?
questions.explanation: Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 9 = 63$ cm². Forgetting the half gives 126.

questions.stem: The number of goals a team scored in 8 games was 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 4, 2, 2. What is the mode?
questions.explanation: 2 appears four times, more than any other value.

questions.stem: A car uses 7.5 litres of fuel per 100 km. How many litres does it use for a 360 km trip?
questions.explanation: $360 \div 100 = 3.6$ lots of 100 km, and $3.6 \times 7.5 = 27$ litres.

questions.stem: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. What is its circumference, in centimetres, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: $C = \pi d = \pi \times 10 \approx 31.4$ cm. Using the radius in $\pi d$ gives 15.7.

questions.stem: Which is equal to $\frac{6^7}{6^4}$?
questions.explanation: When dividing powers of the same base, subtract the indices: $7 - 4 = 3$.

questions.stem: A survey of 200 people found that 64 prefer cycling. What percentage prefer cycling?
A rectangular prism is 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 3 cm high. What is its volume?
questions.explanation: $V = 8 \times 5 \times 3 = 120$ cm³. 16 is the sum of the three dimensions, and 40 is the area of the base only.

questions.stem: A bike costs \$650. Its price rises by 8%. What is the new price, in dollars?
questions.explanation: $650 \times 1.08 = 702$ dollars. The increase alone is \$52.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed and a fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of a head and a 6?
questions.explanation: The events are independent: $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}$. Adding them gives $\frac{2}{3}$.

questions.stem: A runner covers 400 m in 64 seconds. What is her average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed $= \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \frac{400}{64} = 6.25$ m/s. 0.16 is time divided by distance.

questions.stem: A pattern of tiles grows like this: 4, 7, 10, 13, ... Which rule gives the number of tiles $T$ in step $n$?
questions.explanation: The pattern goes up by 3 each step, so $T = 3n + c$. Step 1 has 4 tiles: $3 + c = 4$, so $c = 1$.

questions.stem: Which is the value of $(3 \times 10^5) \times (4 \times 10^{3})$ in scientific notation?
questions.explanation: $3 \times 4 = 12$ and $10^5 \times 10^3 = 10^8$, giving $12 \times 10^8 = 1.2 \times 10^9$. $12 \times 10^8$ is the right value but not in scientific notation.

questions.stem: A ramp rises 1.2 m over a horizontal distance of 3.5 m. How long is the sloping surface of the ramp, in metres, to one decimal place?
The median of four numbers 3, 8, $x$ and 12 is 9. The numbers are already in order. What is $x$?
questions.explanation: With four numbers, the median is the mean of the middle two: $\frac{8 + x}{2} = 9$, so $8 + x = 18$ and $x = 10$.

questions.stem: The line $y = mx + 3$ passes through the point $(4, 11)$. What is the value of $m$?
questions.explanation: Substitute: $11 = 4m + 3$, so $4m = 8$ and $m = 2$.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite angle $\theta$ is 7 cm and the hypotenuse is 25 cm. Which is the value of $\sin\theta$?
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{7}{25}$. $\frac{24}{25}$ is $\cos\theta$ (the adjacent side is 24 by Pythagoras).

questions.stem: Simplify $\frac{12a^6b^2}{4a^2b}$.
questions.explanation: $12 \div 4 = 3$, $a^6 \div a^2 = a^4$, and $b^2 \div b = b$.

questions.stem:
A test for a rare condition was trialled on 400 people.

| | Has condition | No condition |
|---|---|---|
| Test positive | 18 | 22 |
| Test negative | 2 | 358 |

Of the people who tested positive, what percentage actually had the condition?
questions.explanation: 40 people tested positive ($18 + 22$), and 18 of them had the condition: $\frac{18}{40} = 0.45 = 45\%$.

questions.stem: A cube has a volume of 343 cm³. What is its total surface area, in square centimetres?
questions.explanation: The side is $\sqrt[3]{343} = 7$ cm. Six faces of $7 \times 7 = 49$ cm² give 294 cm².

questions.stem: Ava's pay rose from \$24 to \$27 an hour. What was the percentage increase? Type the number only, without the % sign.
A data set is 5, 6, 6, 7, 8. The value 30 is added. Which statement is true?
options: The median rises more than the mean.
The mean and median rise by the same amount.
Neither the mean nor the median changes.
The mean rises more than the median.
questions.explanation: The mean goes from 6.4 to 10.3. The median goes from 6 to 6.5. An outlier pulls the mean far more than the median.

questions.stem: A photo 10 cm wide and 15 cm tall is enlarged so that it is 24 cm wide. How tall is the enlargement?
questions.explanation: The scale factor is $24 \div 10 = 2.4$, so the height is $15 \times 2.4 = 36$ cm. Adding 14 cm to the height, as was added to the width, gives 29 cm.

questions.stem: Factorise $6x^2 + 9x$.
questions.explanation: The highest common factor of $6x^2$ and $9x$ is $3x$. $3x \times 2x = 6x^2$ and $3x \times 3 = 9x$.

questions.stem: Why is the library changing its opening hours?
options: The library is running out of money.
Fewer books are being returned late.
Staff asked to work on Sundays.
Weekday hours did not suit many people.
questions.explanation: The notice says the change 'follows a survey in which more than half of the people who answered said that weekday opening hours did not suit them'.

questions.stem: What will happen on Mondays from 1 July?
options: The library will close at 5 pm.
The library will stay open until 8 pm.
The library will be closed all day.
The drop box will be locked.
questions.explanation: 'The library will close at 5 pm on Mondays instead of 8 pm.'

questions.stem: Why is the Monday change made?
options: Because few people visit on Mondays
To keep the library's costs the same
Because the survey asked for it
To give staff a longer weekend
questions.explanation: 'To keep costs the same, the library will close at 5 pm on Mondays.' The extra Sunday hours are paid for by shorter Monday hours.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Immediately is immediate + ly, so the e stays, and it starts with a double m.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The [[1]] parked across two spaces.
questions.explanation: Vehicle has a silent h and ends in -cle, like 'article'.

questions.stem:
One word in this sentence is spelled incorrectly. Select it.

He was {{ready}} to {{argue}} his {{arguement}} in {{front}} of the {{class}}.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'argument'. The e of 'argue' is dropped before -ment.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Wednesday keeps the silent d: Wed-nes-day. Saying 'Wed-nes-day' slowly helps.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

We stood in a long [[1]] for the ride.
questions.explanation: Queue is q-u-e-u-e. 'Cue' sounds the same but is a signal or a pool stick.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Un + necessary, so there are two ns, then necessary's one c and double s.

questions.stem:
Which word correctly completes the sentence?

The storm had a big ____ on the town.
questions.explanation: Here a noun is needed (a big ___), and the noun is usually 'effect'. 'Affect' is usually the verb: the storm affected the town.

questions.stem:
Which word correctly completes the sentence?

The students left ____ bags in the hall.
questions.explanation: 'Their' shows belonging. 'There' is a place, and 'they're' means 'they are'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The list of winners [[1]] posted on the noticeboard.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'list', which is singular. 'Of winners' describes it, so the verb is 'was'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: I wanted to swim, the pool was closed.
I wanted to swim the pool, was closed.
I wanted; to swim the pool was closed.
I wanted to swim; the pool was closed.
questions.explanation: Two complete sentences joined by only a comma make a comma splice. A semicolon fixes it.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The two [[1]] uniforms were washed together.
questions.explanation: Two teams own the uniforms. A plural ending in s takes the apostrophe after the s: teams'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

She has [[1]] in the choir since Year 7.
questions.explanation: After 'has', use the past participle: has sung. 'Sang' is the simple past.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

The teacher asked Lena and [[1]] to hand out the books.
questions.explanation: Remove 'Lena and': 'asked me to hand out'. 'Me' is the object of 'asked'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: We need: three things for the hike, water, a map and a hat.
We need three things for the hike, water: a map and a hat.
We need three things; for the hike water, a map and a hat.
We need three things for the hike: water, a map and a hat.
questions.explanation: A colon after a complete clause introduces the list that explains it.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The match was cancelled; the oval was flooded.
The match was cancelled, the oval was flooded.
The match was cancelled the oval, was flooded.
The match; was cancelled the oval was flooded.
questions.explanation: Two related complete sentences can be joined with a semicolon. Joining them with only a comma is a comma splice.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence.

Every one of the players [[1]] a water bottle.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'every one', which is singular, so the verb is 'needs'.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{4}$? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explanation: Common denominator 12: $\frac{8}{12} - \frac{3}{12} = \frac{5}{12}$.

questions.stem: What is $1.5 \times 400$?
What is 20% of 85?
What is $-12 \div (-3) - 5$?
questions.explanation: Divide first: $-12 \div (-3) = 4$ (two negatives give a positive). Then $4 - 5 = -1$.

questions.stem: What is $8 + 12 \div 4 \times 2$?
questions.explanation: Divide and multiply left to right before adding: $12 \div 4 = 3$, $3 \times 2 = 6$, then $8 + 6 = 14$.

questions.stem: Write $\frac{3}{8}$ as a decimal.

questions.explanation: Line up the decimal points: $4.50 + 0.75 = 5.25$.

questions.stem: Which is closest to $\frac{398}{41}$?
questions.explanation: Round to $\frac{400}{40} = 10$.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 eggs for every 2 cups of flour. How many eggs are needed for 8 cups of flour?
questions.explanation: 8 cups is 4 lots of 2 cups, so $4 \times 3 = 12$ eggs.

questions.stem: What is 0.3 as a percentage? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 100: $0.3 \times 100 = 30$, so 30%.

questions.stem: Which is equal to $\frac{18}{24}$?
questions.explanation: Divide top and bottom by 6: $\frac{18}{24} = \frac{3}{4}$.

questions.stem: What is $-4 \times (-5) \times (-1)$?
questions.explanation: $-4 \times (-5) = 20$, and $20 \times (-1) = -20$. An odd number of negative factors gives a negative answer.

questions.stem: What is $\frac{3}{5}$ of 45?
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{5}$ of 45 is 9, so $\frac{3}{5}$ is $3 \times 9 = 27$.

questions.stem: What is $7.2 \div 9$?
Which number is between $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$?
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333$ and $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$. Only 0.4 is between them.

questions.stem: Expand $-4(x - 3)$.
questions.explanation: Multiply each term by $-4$: $-4 \times x = -4x$ and $-4 \times -3 = +12$.

questions.stem: Write $5.6 \times 10^{4}$ as an ordinary number.
questions.explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places right: 56 000.

questions.stem: How many square centimetres are in 1 square metre?
Which is equal to $(x^3)^4$?
questions.explanation: For a power of a power, multiply the indices: $3 \times 4 = 12$.

questions.stem: A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of rice. How many grams are needed for 10 people?
questions.explanation: 300 g for 4 people is 75 g per person, and $75 \times 10 = 750$ g.

questions.stem: Five friends have \$12, \$18, \$9, \$15 and \$21. What is the mean amount, in dollars?
questions.explanation: The total is \$75, and $75 \div 5 = 15$ dollars.
Subtracting a negative is adding: $-8 + 3 = -5$.

questions.stem: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular hexagon?
questions.explanation: The interior angles of a hexagon add to $(6 - 2) \times 180 = 720^\circ$, and $720 \div 6 = 120^\circ$.
Divide both sides by 4: $x + 2 = 9$, so $x = 7$.

questions.stem: A \$60 game is on sale for 15% off. What is the sale price, in dollars?
questions.explanation: 15% of \$60 is \$9, so the sale price is $60 - 9 = 51$ dollars.
